That sounds generous until you count the meetings you would actually record — a sales rep on four calls a day passes it in the first week, and the overage is $0.50 an hour. Unlimited transcription is the real reason to be on Business at $17, so treat Pro as a plan for occasional recording rather than a cheaper version of the same thing. Worth checking before you buy: consent. A recorder that joins every meeting changes what people say in them, and that is a policy decision rather than a pricing one.

video:video.video:title: MigrationPro Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The listing tells you nothing about what this costs. “Free to install. Additional charges may apply”, and a single plan block saying pricing is tailored to the entities you migrate. To learn a number you have to leave the App Store for the vendor's calculator, and the first number you find there — $29 — is the floor for the smallest store on the self-service route, not the price for yours. Their own homepage says a typical store lands between $49 and $299. Run the calculator before you form an opinion about value.
The add-on structure used to be the unknowable part, and as of 18 September 2026 it is not: the pricing page lists every add-on with a price, from $19 to $39, and marks all of them included on the managed plan. That is a real improvement in what a buyer can read before committing. It also makes the self-service route look less like $29 — the 301 redirects add-on, which is the one thing a migrating store can least afford to get wrong, is a $29 extra on a $29 migration.
The marketing still runs ahead of the evidence. The pricing page says “Trusted by 250,000+ stores”, the homepage uses the same figure for migrations, and the FAQ says 250,000+ migrations over 13 years — one number doing three different jobs. The same page claims 5.0 from 170+ verified App Store reviews while the listing itself shows 186, of which 181 are five-star, 4 are four-star and one is a single star. The reviews are genuinely good; weigh them rather than the banner.
One practical limit sits in the reviews rather than the marketing. The FAQ says most stores finish in one to three hours and that 10,000+ products may take longer but still complete the same day, while a merchant migrating a very large catalogue in July 2026 wrote plainly that large volumes take a very long time and that the team helped speed it up. If you are moving tens of thousands of records, let the free demo and your own record count decide which of those two you are, not the FAQ.

video:video.video:title: MindStudio Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The no-markup model pass-through is genuinely fair — but it also means your real cost is subscription PLUS model spend, and an agent that loops or processes big documents burns provider credits invisibly until you set limits. The honest build discipline: start every agent with usage caps, and treat 'no-code' as no-code for the plumbing — the logic design and prompt quality are still entirely on you.

video:video.video:title: Miro Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Per-member pricing charges for every member added to the workspace, so an org-wide rollout multiplies at full headcount — and the free plan's 3-board cap is workspace-wide, not per person, so real teams outgrow it in days. Model who truly needs to edit before you buy seats.

video:video.video:title: Mktg.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest cautions. First, the price is still hidden — a 404 where the pricing page should be, and no pricing item in the navigation — which for a tool that promises spend transparency is an irony worth noticing, and the FAQ makes it sharper: its own introduction says it covers what the platform costs, and then no answer in it names a figure. What the FAQ does publish is the tier names, Growth and Enterprise, and the fact that EU data residency is Enterprise-only. Second, the ROI story is the vendor's own: the homepage tile assumes a $5M budget and puts a 3% efficiency gain at $150K alongside $100K of reallocated spend, which is 2% of the same budget. Ask for verified case numbers at your spend level on the demo call.

video:video.video:title: Modelize Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The economics are flat: at roughly $0.19 to $0.20 an image on every tier, moving up the ladder buys resolution, custom presets and support, never a cheaper image. Read it that way and the pricing is honest; read it as a volume discount and you will overbuy. Two other things deserve a clear head. The output quality rides on Google's Gemini image models rather than on anything Modelize owns, so results and consistency can shift when Google ships a new version, and that is outside the vendor's control as much as yours. And the app is genuinely new — launched 20 April 2026, 25 reviews on 17 September 2026 — so the 4.9 average is a small sample, not a track record. Finally, an on-model photo generated by AI shows a person who does not exist; check what your ad platforms and marketplaces require you to disclose before you build a catalogue on it.

video:video.video:title: Momence Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The 'free' plan is the most expensive one once you have real volume: a 5% commission on every sale overtakes Pro's $60 flat fee around $29k a year in processed revenue, and Pro in turn loses to the $199 Custom plan above about $67k a year. Pick your tier by volume, not by sticker — and note what the middle tier does not include. The tooltip on the Pro card lists the same exclusions as the free plan: no add-ons, no phone number, no inbox, no retail products, no reporting or insights, no staff members, no locations. Pro halves your commission and adds no features.

video:video.video:title: Moosend Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The friendly $7-9 headline is the entry rate at the smallest list size (500 contacts), and the ladder above it does not fall smoothly: paid annually, 8,000 contacts costs $51 a month while 10,000 costs $70, so a list of 9,000 sits on the wrong side of the sharpest jump on the slider. The same reversal repeats at 100,000 and at 600,000. Read the comparison table before you assume Pro covers you, too: transactional emails, SSO and SAML, a dedicated IP, hosted files and an account manager are Moosend+ add-ons or Enterprise rather than included.

video:video.video:title: Motive Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: A pricing page with a form where the prices should be. That is the finding, and it matters more in fleet than in software generally. The real cost here is not a monthly rate: it is hardware per vehicle, a contract term that is usually multi-year, and an early-termination position you will not hear about until you want out. None of that is public. Before the demo call, decide your own numbers: vehicles, contract length you will accept, and what you currently pay per truck. In a quote-only category the first number you hear is anchored to what they think you can pay, not to a rate card.

video:video.video:title: Murf Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is generation hours per YEAR, not per month — 24 hours sounds generous until you count retakes, and regenerating a script three times bills three times. Voice quality is genuinely strong, but the honest test for any TTS is your specific language, names and jargon: generate your hardest paragraph in the trial before subscribing, because demo voices always sound better than your edge cases.

video:video.video:title: NordVPN Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: For a business you're really buying NordLayer, priced per user with a seat minimum. It's solid and easy, but a VPN is one layer of security, not a whole strategy — don't mistake it for endpoint protection.

video:video.video:title: Notify Me Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It does one job — turning out-of-stock moments into recovered sales via back-in-stock and pre-order alerts — and its value is entirely tied to how often you actually sell out. If your catalog rarely goes out of stock, you won't see much return. As with any Shopify app it's another monthly line item and another script on your storefront, so weigh it against the real revenue you're leaking to stock-outs.

video:video.video:title: Omniseo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest cautions. AI search visibility (GEO) is a young, fast-moving category. Tracking how you appear in ChatGPT and other AI answers is genuinely useful signal, but the metrics are far less standardized than classic SEO — and you're paying to monitor a moving target you only partly influence. And the step from Essentials to Professional is a big jump for more channels and prompts. Treat it as an early-mover intelligence tool, not a guaranteed ranking lever.

video:video.video:title: Oneflow Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The entry is €250 a month on annual billing — €3,000 a year committed before you've sent your first contract — and the rest of the ladder lives in a sales conversation. If you only need documents signed, dedicated e-sign tools start at roughly a tenth of that.

video:video.video:title: Outgrow Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two meters at once: content types and pieces gate the lower tiers, and monthly LEAD limits gate the upside. Read the caps rather than the prices — Freelancer Limited allows 250 leads a month, Freelancer Pro 1,000, Essentials 7,500 and Business 50,000 — because per lead, Essentials and Business cost almost the same and the real jump in value is from Pro to Essentials. Also note what money does not fix: Outgrow's branding stays on every plan below Essentials, comes off there only under the small-business programme, and a custom domain is Business-only at $600 a month. Interactive content genuinely converts better than static forms, but only when the calculator or quiz gives real value; a thin quiz wrapped around a lead form fools nobody.

video:video.video:title: Ownr Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest limits. It's Canada-only — provincial incorporation covers Ontario, Alberta, BC and Quebec — so it's no use outside Canada. And it's built for straightforward setups: it won't handle complex share structures, multi-investor shareholder agreements, tax planning, partnerships or non-profits. For those you still want an accountant or lawyer.

video:video.video:title: PDWare Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is genuine enterprise software with enterprise buying: opaque pricing, demo-first sales and implementation effort — appropriate for portfolio offices planning hundreds of resources, overkill below that. The honest pre-purchase question is organizational: resource-first planning only works if your PMO will actually maintain forecasts; the tool formalizes discipline, it can't create it.

video:video.video:title: Pangram Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The unavoidable honest limit of every AI detector, including accurate ones: it is never infallible. It will occasionally flag genuinely human writing as AI (false positives) and miss some AI text, so it must be used as a signal, never as sole proof for high-stakes calls like academic penalties or hiring. Pangram's pitch is fewer false positives than rivals, which is real progress — but 'fewer' is not 'none'. Pair it with human judgment and the credit meter with your actual volume.

video:video.video:title: Papaya Global Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Every headline price is a 'starting from' that dead-ends at 'book a demo'. And multiple reviewers report the real bill runs bigger than the sticker: 30-50% over quote, with setup, FX and filing fees surfacing after signing (reviewer reports, not universal terms). The documented contract is typically a two-year agreement with a rolling 90-day termination clause, so read the term and exit clauses closely before signing. The deeper structural knock is where the work happens. Outside the countries where Papaya owns entities, it delivers EOR through in-country partners; a third-party estimate puts the owned count near 40, and Papaya does not disclose which are owned versus partner. So at 15+ countries you're often one escalation removed from whoever actually runs your payroll. Clients report a recurring set of problems: invoicing errors, data that doesn't sync between Papaya and the partner, and missed or late payroll runs. Support decays from a named account manager into a rotating ticket queue with no live channel.

video:video.video:title: Parim Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Unlimited users sounds like the generous part, and it is — until you notice what replaces per-seat pricing: a bill that scales with shifts scheduled. For a staffing agency or an events business, shift volume is the one number that swings hardest month to month, which makes this the least predictable pricing model in the category. Before you commit, ask for the price at your busiest month rather than your average, and ask what happens when you cross a threshold.

video:video.video:title: Passpack Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The honest trade-off is maturity, not security. The interface is plain, the mobile side is very new, and some users report slow support and billing hiccups. You are trading polish and a settled mobile experience for price and solid zero-knowledge encryption.
Android is the concrete form of that trade. The iOS app arrived on 10 August 2026; twenty-seven days later, on 6 September 2026, there was still no Android app. Passpack's own Downloads menu offered only iOS and the browser extension, and a Google Play search for 'passpack' that day returned thirteen apps, all of them rival password managers and none of them this one. If your team is on Android, plan as though the app does not exist, because it does not.
Their own pages lag their announcements, too, though less than they did. Passpack told partners on 2 September 2026 that TOTP now works on every plan, and on 3 September the word appeared on neither the plans nor the key-features page; by 6 September the plans comparison table lists both TOTP and 'Mobile app for iOS', in the section that carries no plan exclusions. The key-features page has not caught up: on 6 September it still listed 'Mobile & Browser Extensions' under New Features Coming Soon, four weeks after iOS shipped and with the extensions already sold on the plans page. Read the plans table rather than the newsletter, and confirm stored TOTP codes inside the 28-day trial.

video:video.video:title: Payoneer Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The conversion and cross-currency withdrawal markups are where it quietly costs you — for pure currency conversion a specialist like Wise is often cheaper. Payoneer earns its keep on marketplace payouts and getting paid by international clients, less so as an FX tool.

video:video.video:title: Piktochart Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The ladder here is not about how much you make, it is about which file you are allowed to hand over. Pro — the tier the page marks most popular — exports PNG only. PDF and PowerPoint are Business features, which the full feature table confirms in a single row most people scroll past. So if the reason you want this is to email a PDF handout or drop slides into a deck, Pro at $10 a member a month is not a cheaper Piktochart — it is the wrong product. Your real entry price is $17 a member a month on annual billing, or $20 monthly.
The free plan reads as generous and is not. Unlimited projects, two downloads — and not two a month: the comparison table lists the number of downloads as a flat 2. That is enough to find out whether you like the editor, which is a fair trial, but it is not the working free tier some competitors in this category offer, so do not plan around it.
The third thing to price is the AI credits: 60 on Free, 500 on Pro, 1,000 on Business. Nowhere on the pricing page does it say what one credit buys, or what happens when you run out — there is no top-up price anywhere on the page. If AI generation is the reason you are buying, ask what a credit costs and what it covers before you commit to a year, because that is a meter that can decide your bill and it is not published.
One last piece of arithmetic. The annual discount is 33% on Pro but only 15% on Business, so the saving shrinks exactly at the tier most teams that need PDF or PowerPoint end up on. And if you have an educational email address or nonprofit status the picture changes completely: Education is $39.99 per member for a whole year and Nonprofit is $60, against $120 for a year of Pro, and both include the PDF and PowerPoint exports that Pro does not. Read the discount labels on those two with a squint, though. The FAQ calls them 76% and 64% off 'our annual pricing', which works back to about $167 a year — neither the $120 the same FAQ quotes for annual Pro nor the $180 that monthly Pro ann

video:video.video:title: Pippit Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is credits per attempt, not per usable result — and buyer reviews centre on exactly that. Trustpilot reviewers describe generations that failed but still consumed their credits, refunds that were hard to get, and support replies measured in weeks. A tool that charges for its own failures puts the cost of unreliability on you.

video:video.video:title: Pixel Union Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: A premium theme is a strong starting point, not a finished store. The conversion lift comes from how you configure, populate and optimize it -- a $360 theme on a store with weak product pages or slow images still converts weakly. Heavily customized premium themes can also be more work to keep updated and can add page weight if you switch on every feature. Buy it for the design system and speed-to-launch, not as a magic conversion switch.

video:video.video:title: Planday Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The €25 monthly platform fee on Plus is the line most comparisons miss. At the 10-user minimum, Plus is €49.90 in seats plus €25 flat, so €74.90 against €14.95 for five users on Starter — the jump is not from €2.99 to €4.99, it is roughly five times the bill. That fee also does not scale down, so the smaller your team, the larger a share of it you carry. Work out your real per-head cost at your actual headcount before choosing, and check which side of the line leave management and payroll integrations fall on, because those are the two features that usually force the upgrade.

video:video.video:title: Plansom Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The thing you cannot check is the price. plansom.com publishes no figure, /pricing returns 404, and there is no pricing link in the navigation — the only routes to a number are the signup or a sales conversation. The integration list is no longer the weak spot it once was: Claude, ChatGPT, Slack, Gmail, Outlook, Notion, HubSpot, Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Zoom and Fireflies are all named on the homepage, and there is a published Microsoft collaboration behind the Teams work. But it is still the smaller player next to Asana, ClickUp and Motion, and it has repositioned around AI agents that run tasks for you. Agent work is usually metered, so ask what a unit of it costs before you compare anything.

video:video.video:title: Plesk Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest notes. Plesk has been raising prices steadily (the 2026 round averaged ~26%), so budget for the renewal trajectory, not today's invoice — it's a recurring theme in the ecosystem since the acquisition era. And the domain caps are the real tier-driver: growing past 10 or 30 domains bumps you up a license, so count your domains including the parked ones before choosing.

video:video.video:title: Postscript Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $0 a month is not free — it carries a $49 monthly minimum spend, which means $49 is your floor whether you send anything or not. Read the tiers as what they are: a platform fee plus a per-message rate plus carrier fees. That third line is easy to miss because it sits in a footnote rather than on the tier cards, and it is not small: the page puts the average US carrier fee at $0.00418 an SMS and $0.00841 an MMS, so against the $0.009 volume rate on Starter it adds close to half again. Before you compare this with anything, work out your monthly message volume and multiply it out on all three published tiers: Growth costs $100 more than Starter but saves a fifth of a cent per message, so it pays back somewhere around 50,000 messages a month.

video:video.video:title: Prezi Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It exports to PDF only — no editable .pptx — and the zooming format is polarising: some audiences find it engaging, others find it disorienting.

video:video.video:title: Pricefy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Credit where due: the free tier is real. But the first paid step is a cliff — $0 straight to $99 — and price updates run at most twice a day even on Enterprise, so this is rules-based repricing, not marketplace-speed. The headline prices are monthly rates; the advertised savings require annual commitment.

video:video.video:title: Printify Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Printify makes nothing until you sell — the Premium fee only pays off past a break-even order volume, and because it's a middleman marketplace, print quality and shipping vary by the provider you pick. Order samples first.

video:video.video:title: Process Street Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Pricing is opaque and jumps steeply from Startup to Pro, with seat minimums that push the real cost above the headline per-member rate — you'll need a sales call to price it. Best once recurring checklists are core to how you operate.

video:video.video:title: ProtectMyOrder Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Start with what is no longer there. Read on 18 September 2026, the Shopify App Store listing for this app is gone: the page says it is not currently available and sends support questions to the vendor. The vendor's site is still live and still selling, and its own footer still links to that dead page. The way in is now a form and a collaborator-access request rather than an install button, and the $20 monthly minimum — which only ever appeared on the App Store plan — no longer appears anywhere a buyer can read it.
That removes the discrepancy this review was first built around and leaves a harder one. Everything you can now learn about what this costs sits on a page the vendor controls, and all three tiers take a share of your upsell revenue rather than a fee. On Standard the pitch is that you keep 80%, and whether that is profit is settled by your own loss rate: a missing parcel is your replacement, your postage and your conversation.
The public record has thinned with the listing. Twelve reviews sat on it in August, most of them from 2024, and while it is down that record is not readable at all — the revenue figures merchants quote on the vendor's own site are theirs and unaudited. Selling package protection also brushes against insurance rules in some jurisdictions. The vendor says its arrangement has been verified with US and UK insurance lawyers, which is their statement rather than a regulator's; if you trade where that matters, ask your own adviser what you are allowed to sell before you turn it on.

video:video.video:title: PushOwl Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The bundles are push-first: every paid tier still caps included email at 500 a month, so 'omnichannel' email at any real volume means buying separate credits — and consumption-based pricing gets harder to predict as your sends climb. It's also Shopify-exclusive, so it becomes a dead end the day you move platforms.

video:video.video:title: Pythago Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $39 headline is the per-store price once you run three-plus stores — a single store is actually $59 a month. And because it is priced per store, every store you add adds a full subscription: scaling your operation scales the bill linearly, with no volume break below three stores.

video:video.video:title: Qoyod Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The entry tier does not do the thing the product is sold on. Qoyod's pitch is surviving Saudi e-invoicing, but Basic covers ZATCA Phase 1 only — Phase 2 is the integration phase, where invoices are cleared with the tax authority in real time, and that starts at Pro. If Phase 2 applies to you, your actual floor is 1,800 SAR and not 1,200. The second thing to price before you sign: Basic is genuinely one user and one location, and every extra seat is 240 SAR a year, which is a fifth of the whole Basic plan per person. A four-person shop on Basic pays 1,200 + 3×240 = 1,920 SAR, more than Pro costs while still sitting on Phase 1. Add a single POS user at 600 SAR and the arithmetic tips further. Work out your seat and location count first, then pick the tier — doing it the other way round is how the add-on line becomes the biggest number on the invoice.

video:video.video:title: QuickSigner Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: A few users report occasional email-deliverability hiccups — otherwise it does exactly what it says (recipients even sign without an account) for a fraction of enterprise pricing.

video:video.video:title: QuillBot Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free tier is deliberately narrow: 125 words per paraphrase and two of the modes. The honest framing is that this is a box of writing utilities -- paraphraser, grammar, plagiarism, AI detection -- rather than somewhere you actually write. General AI chat tools now overlap much of it. Note the sticker too: the advertised €8.33 a month assumes you pay for the year, and month-to-month is €19.95, about 2.4 times as much.

video:video.video:title: Reclaim.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The magic only works on a calendar it can write to. Google Calendar was first, but Microsoft 365, Outlook.com and Exchange-backed accounts are supported too (reclaim.ai/integrations/outlook-calendar, read 15 September 2026); Reclaim's own help centre still lists hosted and on-premise Exchange as unsupported. The free tier is quite limited. A genuine time-saver for the right setup, useless for the wrong one.

video:video.video:title: Replit Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The credit model on AI-heavy building is unpredictable — a complex agent session can burn credits fast, and they expire monthly, so heavy AI users hit surprise costs. Great for learning and prototyping; watch the meter for production work.

video:video.video:title: Restream Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The channel caps are the business model -- each tier buys a few more destinations. Seats are the second meter: Free and Standard include one and cannot buy another at all, while Professional and Business include two and sell extras at $25 a month. Price it at your real destination count and team size, not the sticker.

video:video.video:title: Retouch4me Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Work out which lane you are in before you pay, because the three lanes price the same photo very differently. One plugin forever at $145 is honest value — but a working portrait stack means four plugins at $145-$179 each, $648 in total, while the Start subscription hands you the entire set for $169 a year with 2,400 retouches included. The catch cuts the other way too: own-forever versus keep-paying is the real decision, since the credits' 5-year rollover only holds 'while the subscription is active' — stop paying and the suite and the stockpile are gone. Low volume? Cloud retouching without a subscription is sold in packs, $24 for 100 retouches, and at $0.15 to $0.24 a photo it is the dearest lane per image, not the cheapest.

video:video.video:title: Riverside Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is not recording time, it is separate-track download time — and separate tracks are the entire reason to use this rather than a video call. Recording itself is unlimited. Their own FAQ on hitting the cap: you can still access your content but cannot download new separate tracks until the next billing cycle or you upgrade. So a busy interview month does not cost you more money, it quietly stops you delivering, which is worse. Fifteen hours on Pro is about seven or eight hour-long interviews once you count retakes and the recording that runs while you set up. There is a 14-day trial rather than a published free plan.

video:video.video:title: Runpod Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest math is utilization. On the same card serverless runs roughly 1.6-2x the pod rate per compute-hour: $4.79 against $2.89 for an H100, $2.72 against $1.39 for an A100 PCIe. That is brilliant for spiky inference and wasteful for steady training, so pick the mode per workload, not per habit. And like all GPU clouds, the meter never sleeps: an idle pod you forgot is the cloud version of the subscription graveyard. Set spend alerts before the first experiment, not after the first invoice.

video:video.video:title: SEO Space Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Squarespace has been quietly absorbing the job this tool was invented for. The platform's own SEO panel, checklist, sitemaps and structured data are free, and its AI-suggested titles, descriptions and alt text are available on Fluid Engine 7.1. On 7 July 2026 it announced AI Visibility, brand tracking across AI search, included on 7.1 plans with no extra subscription. It is metered against plan-varying AI credits rather than unlimited. If you own a single Squarespace site, a large share of what you would pay for here is now a friendlier wrapper around something the platform already does. The tool earns its keep on volume and client work, not on one site. Note too what the disclaimer under their own plan cards says out loud — “All plans include every feature. No artificial restrictions.” — so moving up the ladder buys site slots, not a better tool. One thing arrived after that promise, though: Orbit, a five-agent AI layer added since August, sits on its own card as a second subscription at $119 a month or $952 a year (read 16 September 2026), so the feature that is currently being marketed hardest is the one no plan includes.

video:video.video:title: SEOmatic Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
This app is eleven years old and has 114 reviews. That is the number to sit with. On the same listing page Shopify shows three direct rivals. SEOLab is 5.0 over 2,368 reviews and free, Tiny SEO 5.0 over 2,261 and free to install, and Smart SEO 4.9 over 851 with a free plan. All three carry between seven and twenty times the review volume, all are rated higher, and none of them charges by product count. SEOmatic's 4.4 is a real rating from real merchants, but it is the weakest track record on its own page.
The distribution behind that 4.4 matters too: 81% five stars against 8% one star, with almost nothing in the middle. The most substantial recent review, from March 2025, is a merchant of six months saying it appears to work on images and nothing else, and that support is difficult and slow. The vendor replied that the reports do exist, and asked them to get in touch. An older one-star from a merchant who lasted seventeen minutes reads 'Paid for it to tell me 0% savings'. Both are about the same thing — what the app actually did after installation was not visible to the person paying for it.
And the product cap is a hard ceiling, not a soft one. There is no tier above 5,000 products on the listing or on seomatic.io, so if your catalogue is larger than that, the published ladder simply does not have a row for you.

video:video.video:title: SMTP.com Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's a veteran, reliable relay, but two honest notes. Pricing is volume-tiered, so a shared IP on the cheapest plan is fine for low volume while serious senders need the dedicated-IP tiers (and the IP warm-up discipline that comes with them). And the value-add features — reputation and verification — are metered on top at ~20% of plan cost, so the real bill is higher than the base tier. It's infrastructure, not a marketing suite; you bring the campaigns.

video:video.video:title: SMTP2GO Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's the pragmatic middle of email infrastructure: simpler and better-supported than the hyperscale APIs, cheaper than most, with genuinely useful reporting — but sending reputation is still yours to earn. A relay delivers what your domain deserves: without proper SPF/DKIM/DMARC and list hygiene, no provider saves you. Check the overage rate for your tier before you size up: on the 10,000 plan an extra thousand emails costs $1.20 against the $1.50 a thousand you already pay, and the 50,000 plan at $30 works out cheaper per email than Professional at $75.

video:video.video:title: Salesflare Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's deliberately lean: no built-in dialer, no quoting or invoicing, and reporting feels basic unless you export. Integrations cover the essentials (Gmail, Outlook, Zapier) but niche tools lean on Zapier — and at higher seat counts the price overlaps fuller CRMs.

video:video.video:title: Salesflow Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The per-seat rate falls with team size but the monthly bill does not follow it: 19 seats on Starter is $1,330 while 20 seats on Pro is $799, so a team that stops one seat short of a tier pays $531 a month more for less. The same cliff sits at 49-to-50 seats and again at 99-to-100. And the monthly quotas are the real ceiling: 400 invites and 800 Open InMails is a fixed budget, not a starting point.

video:video.video:title: SaneBox Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It works with any email provider, which is a genuine advantage over the built-in tools in Gmail and Outlook. But you are paying monthly to filter mail that modern clients increasingly sort for free. The value is real only if your inbox is genuinely overwhelming and native filters are not cutting it. Price it on the plan you would actually keep: the headline rate is a two-year commitment, and month to month the same Snack plan is $9.49 rather than $4.54.

video:video.video:title: Seamless.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Data accuracy is the recurring complaint — independent tests put email deliverability around 74% (20–30% bounce) versus ZoomInfo's ~2–3%, so real cost per usable contact climbs. The buying experience is the other weak spot: sales-led, auto-renew with 30–60 day written cancellation, and reports of charges after a 'confirmed' cancellation.

video:video.video:title: Section Library Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Almost three years on the App Store and one review. The app launched 10 October 2023 and, as of 17 September 2026, exactly one merchant has written about it: a five-star note from October 2023 by someone who had it installed for four minutes. That is not evidence of quality and not evidence of trouble — it is an absence of evidence, and on an app that writes sections into your live theme, that absence is the main thing to weigh. On the same listing page Shopify shows Section Store with 2,929 reviews, also free to install, which is what a track record looks like in this category. And on 17 September 2026 the vendor’s own site, sectionlibrary.com, answered with Shopify’s “Store unavailable” page instead of a website.
Second, the credit is undefined. Every plan is priced in credits and nothing on the listing says what one buys, so you cannot price your own usage before you commit.
Third, the AI half of the product is Google's. Sections are generated by Gemini 3.1 Pro, so output quality and consistency shift when Google ships a new model, which is outside the vendor's hands as much as yours. The library half — the 200+ pre-built sections — is the part that depends on nobody else, and it is the part worth judging the app on.

video:video.video:title: Securify Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Blocking by country and IP is a blunt instrument and it cuts both ways: every rule that keeps out a fraudster also keeps out a customer travelling, using a corporate VPN, or living behind a carrier NAT. The app is honest enough to give you a live log of what it blocked, and that log is the part to actually read — a rule set nobody reviews quietly costs sales. Also worth separating in your head: blocking bots from your analytics is a reporting fix, while blocking fraud at checkout is a money fix, and the two need different rules.

video:video.video:title: Seel Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two things to weigh, and neither is the price you pay — because you do not pay one. First, you cannot set the fee. Seel's algorithm prices it, so if it lands too high for your niche and shoppers stop opting in, your only lever is switching the feature off entirely. Second, the charge appears on your checkout, not Seel's: shopper-side complaints filed with the BBB describe the fee arriving in the cart with the opt-out easy to miss, and that lands on your brand. Test it as a customer before you enable it. Also check the platform list — Shopify, BigCommerce and Adobe Commerce only, with no WooCommerce, Wix or custom storefront support.

video:video.video:title: Selixer Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Read the feature lists rather than the prices and the entry tier stops looking like the product. Essence at $149 a month gives you two seats, one connected ad platform, a year of history and an inventory health score. The full True Profit waterfall, the per-product P&L and the POAS and CAC tracking — the reason anyone installs a profit dashboard — all start on Catalyst at $299. So the real price of what this app is sold on is double the headline.
The ad-platform caps decide the tier as much as the features do: one, then two, then three. If you run Meta, Google and TikTok you are on the $399 plan for connectivity alone, whatever your revenue looks like.
The monthly figure is also not the whole bill. Each plan carries an AI credit allowance — 500, 2,000 and 3,000 — and the listing sells top-ups from $25, with usage-based charges billed on the same 30-day cycle. Find out what spends a credit before you budget around the headline.
And this is a new app. It launched on 19 May 2026 and has one public review. There is nothing bad in the record, but there is barely any record, and this is a tool you hand your cost prices, your ad spend and your margins to. Use the 14-day trial to reconcile its numbers against a month you have already closed in your own books before you trust a dashboard you cannot yet audit.

video:video.video:title: Sellfy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest mechanic is the revenue ladder: plans cap by your ANNUAL SALES, so success moves you up. But the caps are soft - Sellfy's FAQ says it may charge 2% on revenue above your limit rather than forcing an upgrade, so ask whether that applies to you before jumping a tier. The 0% transaction fee is genuinely rare and beats percentage-taking platforms at volume; below a few hundred in monthly sales the flat subscription is the tax instead, and your processor still takes about 2.9% + 30c regardless.

video:video.video:title: Sendcloud Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing has layers — a per-label fee on top of the subscription, plus carrier surcharges that can land on invoices weeks later. It's built out-of-the-box, so deep customisation is limited, there's no inventory management (ShipStation has it), and high-volume shippers (€12k+/mo) plus pickup-reliability complaints suggest it's happiest with small-to-mid EU stores.

video:video.video:title: Sentaro Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The category claim (AI catches what filters miss) is plausible — Microsoft/Google native filtering misses sophisticated BEC — but any vendor's accuracy percentage is measured on their own test set, not your mail flow. The honest procurement move: run their trial alongside your current filtering, count real catches and false positives for two weeks, and price per mailbox against the incumbents with that data in hand.

video:video.video:title: Serpstat Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The thing you are actually buying is data coverage, and that is the one thing you cannot verify — Serpstat's own published figures do not agree with each other. Re-read on 24 July 2026, their homepage says 529 billion backlinks, their data hub says 1.1 trillion, and their backlinks page says 1.7 trillion in the prose while its own spec block on that same page says 1.1 trillion. The keyword count reads 8.62 billion on one page and 7.46 billion on another. That is not evidence the data is thin; it is evidence that these numbers cannot serve as a basis for your decision. Judge it on your own searches during the trial instead. Two other things to weigh. Backlink reports are capped at 10,000 results per report on Team, Team x2 and Agency alike, so paying from $129 to $499 buys more of everything except a deeper backlink report. And 'maximum pages to scan' in a single crawl (5,000 / 25,000 / 50,000) is a far smaller number than the monthly 'pages to audit' allowance it sits next to.

video:video.video:title: ServiceM8 Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Unlimited users on every paid tier is genuinely unusual in this category and worth saying first: put your whole crew in without the bill moving. The meter is jobs instead, and jobs are the thing you least control. Fifty a month on Starter is roughly two a working day, which a two-van operation passes in a busy month — and the next step is not a small one, it is $29 to $79. Count your jobs in your best month rather than your average, because that is the month that will bump you, and a seasonal trade will spend part of the year paying for a tier it does not need. The free tier at 30 jobs and one user is a real trial, not a plan.

video:video.video:title: Shiftie Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's focused, affordable rota software — which means it does scheduling, clock-ins, leave and swaps well, but it isn't a full HR or payroll platform, so a growing business will still bolt on payroll and HR tools around it. Pricing is genuinely low, but the per-active-employee model means a large seasonal team in a busy month costs more than the headline suggests. For shift-based scheduling specifically, it's a clean, cheap fit.

video:video.video:title: Shippo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing is honest but layered. The free tier stops at 30 labels a month, and its 5¢ per label on your own carrier accounts quietly adds up. Pro looks like a flat $17 a month until you read the comparison table: it covers up to 10,000 shipments and then bills $0.08 for every label beyond that, so a good sales month adds a variable line to a subscription that reads as fixed. Address validation outside the US is metered too, at 9¢, 8¢ or 6¢ depending on plan. The real money is elsewhere anyway — in the carrier rate discounts, which vary by lane and weight. Run your five most common shipments through it against your current rates; that comparison decides, not the subscription price.

video:video.video:title: Shorby Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: In a category where the market leader has a generous free plan, Shorby charges from day one, so it has to earn the gap. Its case rests on two genuinely differentiated features: messenger deep-links, one tap into WhatsApp/Telegram chats, and retargeting pixels firing on every click. If you use neither, Linktree's free tier wins; if messenger-first selling or ad retargeting is your funnel, the $15 pays for itself.

video:video.video:title: Shore Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's built for local appointment businesses, and that's also the boundary: the integration list is short (calendar, Google, Instagram, Meta), and once you add POS and payments the monthly total climbs well past the entry price. If you only need a booking link, this is more machine than you need.

video:video.video:title: SignNow Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's built for straightforward everyday signing — if you need deep contract-lifecycle (CLM) features, a heavier platform fits better.

video:video.video:title: Signeasy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $10 Personal plan is annual-billed and single-seat — and note that sign-unlimited is not send-unlimited: proper unlimited sending starts at Business, $20 per seat on a yearly commitment, while contract-management features gate at Business Pro, $30 per seat.

video:video.video:title: SimpleTexting Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The credit model plus US carrier (10DLC) fees and per-number/per-seat add-ons mean the sticker isn't the whole bill — and SMS marketing only works with genuine opt-in and a real offer, not blasting a cold list.

video:video.video:title: SimplyBook.me Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The plan ladder is set by bookings per month and by how many custom features you may switch on, and those two ceilings move independently — so you can outgrow a plan on features while nowhere near the booking cap, or the reverse. Free and Basic also carry SimplyBook.me branding on your booking page; white-label starts at Premium.

video:video.video:title: SmartSuite Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's a broad, do-everything work-management platform, so the power comes with a learning curve and a per-seat cost that adds up for bigger teams — a single source of truth if you commit, overkill if you just need a task list.

video:video.video:title: Smartli Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Smartli bundles nine AI tools — copy, SEO, images, logos — into one suite, and that breadth is also the honest catch: each individual tool is competent rather than best-in-class, so a team that leans hard on one job may outgrow it toward a specialist. And like all AI copy, its product descriptions and ad copy need a human edit and a fact-check — never publish specs or claims it invents about your product. For a store that wants many content jobs handled cheaply in one place, it's efficient.

video:video.video:title: SocialBee Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You are billed per social profile, not per person, and a profile is one brand account on one network. A single business posting to Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, X and TikTok has used the whole Bootstrap allowance before a second brand or a client exists. The second thing is that people cost extra on top: Bootstrap and Accelerate are single-user plans, so a two-person team on eight profiles is $49 plus $10, not $29. Count your profiles across every network first — that number, not your team size, decides the tier.

video:video.video:title: Softr Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Builder seats are billed on top of the plan, and pricing counts builders and app users separately, so a public-facing app with a lot of end users gets expensive fast. Watch the overage rate as well as the plan: extra app users are $1 a month on Pro but $2 on Business, so the dearer plan meters growth at double the rate. It fits internal tools and client portals with a known audience, not an open signup.

video:video.video:title: Spocket Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Spocket's pitch is faster-shipping US and EU suppliers, and that's real — but you still pay twice: the monthly subscription and the wholesale product cost, so margins depend on picking items with room to mark up. Catalog breadth is narrower than giant AliExpress-based tools (that's the trade for vetting and shipping speed), and the low Starter product cap pushes serious stores up to Pro quickly. It reduces, not removes, the usual dropshipping risks.

video:video.video:title: Stampezee Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The category is honest and proven (digital stamp cards beat lost paper cards), and the platform is young with limited public pricing and review coverage — so start on the free plan, run one real campaign, and measure repeat-visit lift before paying. The deeper truth of loyalty programs: the mechanics are 10% of the outcome; a reward worth returning for is the other 90%.

video:video.video:title: StoreSEO Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Know what an SEO app can and cannot do before you buy any tier. This one fixes the mechanical layer well — meta titles and descriptions in bulk, alt text, compressed images, JSON-LD, sitemaps, indexing requests — and none of that creates demand for products nobody is searching for. It is maintenance, not marketing, and on a catalogue of 25 products the free tier already does most of it. Two specifics worth a raised eyebrow. The pricing gap between Essential at $39.99 for 250 products and Advanced at $249.99 for 10,000 is filled by a $99.99 Growth plan. That plan lives on the vendor's own site but not on the App Store listing our link points to, which is a strange place to hide a tier. And the AEO/GEO features — the LLMs.txt generator, the Agents.md editor, the separate “agentic” ranking — are a bet, not a channel. No major search or AI vendor has committed to reading llms.txt, so treat those numbers as a hypothesis you are testing rather than traffic you are buying.

video:video.video:title: Storylane Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The jump from Starter to Growth is $50 to $625 a month — twelve and a half times — and the free tier is capped at one live demo, so the moment you want a second demo published you are on the ladder. What is actually being sold at each step is visitor de-anonymisation: 250 a month on Starter, 2,500 on Growth, 10,000 on Premium. Price that against what you already pay a separate tool to do, because it is the meter that decides your tier, not the number of demos. Extra seats are charged on top at $40 to $100 each, which means a five-person sales team on Starter is not $50 a month, it is $210.

video:video.video:title: Streak Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pitch — CRM living inside Gmail — is also the ceiling: everything happens in the inbox, which power users love and growing teams outgrow (reporting, permissions, cross-team process). And note the trajectory: the free tier is gone and per-seat prices sit at real-CRM levels now, so the 'lightweight Gmail add-on' framing no longer matches the invoice. If the inbox is truly where your deals live, few tools feel this natural.

video:video.video:title: Success.co Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The ladder rewards size rather than commitment: moving from 25 to 26 users drops the rate a dollar, and the annual discount is worth about the same single dollar per user. So the number that decides your bill is headcount, not billing term — and at the small end, where most teams start, $12 a user is the least favourable rate on the whole page. The two capabilities a security team will ask for first, SSO and SCIM, are not in any plan: they are $250 a month each, which on a 20-person account doubles the bill.

video:video.video:title: Sunsama Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing page contradicts itself: the plan card says $17 yearly and $22 monthly, the FAQ on the same page says $20 yearly and $25 monthly. One of those is stale, and until you know which, treat $25 as the number you might actually be charged. That is an odd thing to have to say about a company that goes out of its way on that same page to explain why it refuses to use $24.99 pricing — the transparency is real and so is the inconsistency. The other thing to be clear about is that this is per person with no team discount mentioned: two people is two subscriptions, and their own example says $50.

video:video.video:title: Superfiliate Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The price is the part you cannot check. Their pricing page returns 404 with and without www, the homepage carries no figure at all, and the only route to a number is a sales call — so the honest warning is not that it is expensive, but that you cannot compare it against anything until you have spoken to them. Ask for the figure in writing on that call, and ask what separates the ends of whatever range they quote. On fit rather than price: this is built for brands already running creator and affiliate programs, and it is overkill if you are testing your first affiliate offer.

video:video.video:title: SurveyMonkey Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free tier is a teaser. Response caps trigger $0.15-per-response overages that become a hidden cost on big studies. Branding and customisation are limited, and a lot of the good analytics and logic sit behind higher tiers.

video:video.video:title: SurveySparrow Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The conversational-survey UX is the draw, but response limits on lower tiers and the 'contact sales' wall on advanced features (API, higher volume) make budgeting fiddly — and there's no true monthly billing.

video:video.video:title: Survicate Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The plan is metered by response volume, not by surveys — a viral NPS month can push you a tier up, and the free plan's 30-day retention quietly deletes your history. Mind the billing asymmetry too: Starter is monthly-only while Growth and up expect an annual commitment.

video:video.video:title: Switcher Studio Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The app runs on Mac and iOS only — Android phones can join as cameras, but there is no Windows version — so the machine doing the switching has to be an Apple one. And wireless multi-cam is only as reliable as your venue's Wi-Fi; a shaky connection is the failure mode nobody markets. The monetization features (pay-per-view, subscriptions) are genuinely strong, but only matter if you're actually selling access.

video:video.video:title: Synthesia Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The video-minute caps are tight — 10 min/mo on Starter goes fast when you iterate, and re-generating edits burns minutes. Fantastic for avatar-led training and explainers without a studio, but not for high-volume or cinematic production.

video:video.video:title: Tapita AI SEO Blog Builder Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Publishing volume is the trap this tool makes cheap. It generates posts quickly and schedules them daily or weekly in bulk, and a Shopify blog filled with unedited AI articles is precisely the pattern search engines have spent the last two years demoting: the app lowers the cost of production, not the bar for ranking. Used the other way round, as a drafting and structuring tool for posts you actually edit, it is sensible.
The price is the second thing to watch, and on 19 September 2026 there is none to read. The listing publishes no plan block and gives its pricing as Free. That is not the same as free being the whole story: the features it advertises — AI generation, bulk creation, translation, scheduling — were metered in credits until August, and no credit allowance or overage rate is stated anywhere on the page now. The same developer's other listing still prints a complete ladder, so this one is not simply a developer who does not publish prices. Go in expecting to ask what the limits are, and do not plan a content calendar around an allowance nobody has told you the size of.

video:video.video:title: Tapstitch Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Printify is cheaper, higher-margin and has a far bigger catalogue — if you're optimising for profit per sale or product breadth, that's the real trade-off. Tapstitch earns its place when garment quality and brand feel matter more than squeezing the last point of margin.

video:video.video:title: Tax1099 Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Per-form pricing is genuinely cheap for a handful of 1099s, but it's metered: TIN matching, W-9 requests, state filing and corrections can each carry their own charge. A business filing across many recipients and states should tally the add-ons, not just the headline per-form rate. It's a filing tool, not a bookkeeping system; it assumes your payee data is already clean.

video:video.video:title: TaxCycle Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is professional preparer software priced for firms, not a consumer filing app: the cost only makes sense if you're preparing returns for clients at volume. The suites start at about CAD $1,600 a year for one user and each extra seat adds several hundred dollars, so a two- or three-person practice should budget the suite price plus seats, plus GST or HST, before comparing it with per-return alternatives.

video:video.video:title: Team Pulse Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The tiers gate on TWO axes at once — member count and project/pipeline count — so you can hit a wall on either. The CRM pipeline is a big part of the pitch, but it doesn't exist below the $79 Growth plan (Free and Starter have none), and member limits are tight: Starter is a single seat, Growth just three. The listed rates also assume annual billing.

video:video.video:title: Teikametrics Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Read the Advanced tier carefully, because it is not a subscription — it is a subscription plus a percentage. Three per cent of ad spend above $10,000 means a seller spending $40,000 a month pays an extra $900 on top of whatever the custom base is, and that line scales with the thing the product is supposed to make more efficient. That is not automatically wrong — it aligns them with your growth — but it does mean your bill rises when your advertising does, and you should model it at your expected spend rather than your current one. The $10K threshold is the number to watch: crossing it changes the pricing model, not just the price.

video:video.video:title: Tellent Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Tellent's modular shape is genuinely useful — you can buy just the ATS, or just the HRIS — but nothing is priced in public: every tier on tellent.com/pricing ends in 'Get a demo' (read in a browser on 9 September 2026), and recruitee.com/pricing carries no figures either. Ask for Start, Advance and Optimize quoted together with their renewal prices, because you have no anchor to check a single number against. And as with every ATS, workflow fit — approval chains, careers-site needs, integrations with your assessment tools — matters more than the feature list; the free trial is enough to run one real vacancy through, so do that.

video:video.video:title: Tenable Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Note on how we link this one, updated 28 Jul 2026: between 21 and 28 July our partner link was dead — Tenable's shop subdomain stopped resolving, so we pointed the link at Tenable's own product page and earned nothing from it. Tenable confirmed on 28 July that the links are repaired; we re-tested them that day and the link now works again, lands on the same Nessus product page, and does pay us a commission. This is serious, enterprise-grade security tooling with an enterprise price and a learning curve — not a set-and-forget scanner. You need someone who can act on the findings, or you're paying for reports nobody reads.

video:video.video:title: Thordata Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Everything is a meter — per GB, per IP, per 1K responses — so the bill scales with usage. And every rate the site advertises is the largest package on its ladder: $0.65 a GB means buying 5,000 GB, while 1 GB of the same product costs $2.00. Budget at your own volume, not at the headline. Plus the category-wide caveat we'd give any residential-proxy vendor: those '100M+ real residential IPs' come from consumer devices, so check sourcing ethics and your target sites' terms before building on it.

video:video.video:title: Thryv Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two published tiers, $85 and $340, and nothing between them. That makes the decision unusually blunt: not which plan fits, but whether a fourfold step is worth taking all at once. And price the commitment from what the page actually says, which is less than you would like — it prints both annual figures per month, states only that the year saves 15%, and never says whether the term is charged up front. Before that call, list which of the bundled parts you would otherwise buy separately: Thryv's case rests on replacing four or five tools, and if you only want two of them the arithmetic usually favours keeping them. Worth knowing too that the Boosts services, the part sold hardest, cannot be attached to Starter at all.

video:video.video:title: TiXel Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The rating is the most useful number on this listing, but not for the reason an average usually is. Read on 18 September 2026 it is 4.6 across 93 reviews, and the shape behind it is 84 five-star, 3 four-star, nothing at three or two, and 6 one-star. A month earlier it was 4.1 across 78, with 7 at the bottom. Nothing sits in the middle on either reading. That is not a mediocre product; it is a binary one — it works immediately, or it installs cleanly and then tracks nothing at all.
The one-star reviews describe the same failure in the same words: the pixel is set up by the instructions, no page views or add-to-carts ever arrive, and support does not reply. We cannot verify what happened in any individual account, but the consistency of the complaint is itself information.
What is new since August is that the developer now answers them in public. A reply dated 2 September 2026 attributes the empty data to manual pixel configuration, where one mismatched ID or event setting is enough to stop events being recorded at all, and says that step is no longer needed: TiXel now integrates officially with Meta and TikTok and links the pixel to your ad account automatically. That is the vendor's account of its own worst reviews, so treat it as a claim to test rather than a fix to trust. It is at least a specific and checkable one, and the trial has gone from three days to seven, which is enough room to check it.

video:video.video:title: TicketTailor Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The fee honesty is the product — flat cents per ticket instead of percentage skims makes it dramatically cheaper than the big platforms on higher-priced tickets (a $0.30-0.85 fee on a $50 ticket vs a percentage is no contest). The trade: you bring your own audience. There's no discovery marketplace pushing your event, so if you rely on a platform's browsing traffic to sell out, the cheap fees won't fill seats.

video:video.video:title: Todoist Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free plan's 5-project cap, and reminders that fire only at the moment a task comes due, push most serious users to Pro quickly — but Pro is genuinely cheap. It's a personal/team task manager, not a full project platform, so don't expect Gantt-level PM.

video:video.video:title: Toggl Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Toggl's honesty problem is the good kind: the free tier is so capable that many teams never need to pay — the paid line is drawn exactly at 'do you bill clients' (budgets, rates, profitability). If you do, Starter earns itself fast; if you track time for personal discipline, resist the upgrade. Time tracking's real cost everywhere is adoption: the tool is frictionless, but the habit still has to be built.

video:video.video:title: Tradify Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Per-user pricing is honest and simple, but it means the cost scales linearly with headcount — a ten-person crew is a real monthly number, not the single-seat sticker. It's purpose-built for trades job management (quoting, scheduling, invoicing), so it's not a general project-management or accounting suite; you'll still run Xero or QuickBooks alongside it. For a trades business that's a feature, not a flaw.

video:video.video:title: Trainerize Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The client-count ladder looks gentle, but the add-ons are flat and they land hardest on the smallest coach: at five seats a $23 Pro plan dressed with nutrition, payments and video is $88, while the same three turn the $275 two-hundred-client row into $340. Price the stack you'll actually coach with, and note that the branded app is $169 to Trainerize plus a $99/year Apple Developer Account billed by Apple. That said, the client experience and ABC ecosystem are genuinely mature; churn-prone coaches lose more to a clunky app than to a fair subscription.

video:video.video:title: Trainual Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You cannot find out what it costs without booking a demo. All four plans — Core, Pro, Premium and Enterprise — are quote-gated, and the single number the pricing page publishes is the one-time implementation fee of $1,000. The same page answers the sizing question plainly, best suited for companies with 25 to 1000 employees, so a small team is being told twice that it is not the buyer here: once by the fit range and once by a setup fee that arrives before the subscription does. Under a handful of staff, a shared doc may do.

video:video.video:title: Turbotic Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's a newer, enterprise-leaning automation platform, so it's less proven with a smaller community than the big names — and the credit-per-execution model means heavy volume needs cost-checking. Verify it integrates with your actual stack first.

video:video.video:title: Typewise Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The bill has two parts and both are published: a base fee from $99 and a resolution rate from $2 (pay as you go) down to $1 with volume packages. The meter is published too — a ticket closed end to end counts as one resolution, a hand-off to a person counts as half, and a ticket passed straight through or flagged is free. So a conversation the AI cannot finish still bills, at half rate, which is fair but worth budgeting for. What the page still does not say is whether a reopened ticket counts again; get that in writing before the trial. The ROI calculator on their site is the vendor's own arithmetic; the pilot is where you replace it with yours.

video:video.video:title: UENI Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's done-for-you, which is the appeal and the catch. DIY editing and customisation are limited, e-commerce and integrations are basic, and the most common complaint is the gap between the 7-day promise and reality — slow design turnaround and patchy communication with the team. Expect some upselling.

video:video.video:title: UltaHost Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's the classic budget-host trade-off, with one thing in its favour. The sticker price is a term commitment, not a monthly rate: the headline figures are the 2-year prices, the discount ladder runs -30% yearly, -40% for two years and -50% for three, and paying monthly gives all of it back. What has changed is the renewal. Each plan card now states it renews at the same rate for another 2 years, so the usual trap of a cheap first term followed by a dear one is at least written down. Read that line on the plan you actually pick, because it is quoted per plan. The headline rates also sit under a running 40%-off sale, so treat the crossed-out price as marketing rather than a baseline. Support is generally fast but can be hit-or-miss depending on which agent picks up your ticket, and it's a smaller, less-established brand than the big managed hosts. It's a value play, not a premium-SLA one.

video:video.video:title: Unbounce Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The entry price is high for a landing-page tool, and the visitor caps bite if a campaign takes off. It's also oddly behind on basics — no URL import, limited file/code management, and still no true AI page generation in 2026.

video:video.video:title: Unleashed Software Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The 100 sales orders a month included on both bundles is the number that decides your bill, not the $399. A wholesaler running 1,500 orders with six users who wants phone support pays $399 for Core, $200 for the order tier, $207 for three extra seats and $99 for Standard support. That is $905 a month, or 2.3 times the headline, before a one-off onboarding fee of at least $449. Support being a paid add-on rather than part of the plan is the detail most comparison tables miss. Price the bundle you will actually be on: count your busiest month's orders, your real seat count, and decide whether you can live without phone support, then compare that total against the alternatives rather than comparing entry prices.

video:video.video:title: UptimeRobot Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The famous free tier is real — but the paid ladder has quiet extras: extra login seats cost $15-19 per month EACH beyond the included ones, and SMS or voice-call alerts are pay-per-credit on every plan. The Solo tier includes no team seats at all.

video:video.video:title: VEA Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pitch is unusually bold: an AI that learns your business the way a great employee would, finds the constraint keeping you stuck, and helps you solve it. That ambition is also the honest caveat — it's a young product making a big promise, its price ladder was rebuilt in August 2026 with a top tier at $597 per user a month, and independent review coverage is still thin. Judge it in the trial on one measurable question: did it identify a constraint you recognize as painfully real? If yes, it earns the next month. If its advice stays generic — the thing its own positioning promises to avoid — walk.

video:video.video:title: VWO Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The jump from Growth to Pro is steep — small businesses get priced out of MVT and complex targeting — and the UI is dense with options. Some users note the reporting breaks more often than pricier tools (though it doesn't affect the tests themselves). The part that costs people money later is what happens to a winner. VWO applies page changes through its SmartCode — their own page says the asynchronous SmartCode “loads page changes asynchronously when the web page loads” — so a variant left running in the editor is rendered by VWO rather than built into your site. Fine while you pay, gone when you stop. Their server-side testing changes the arithmetic here, because those changes live in your own stack; the client-side ones do not.

video:video.video:title: Velora Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Velora is three acquired products (Keela, Aplos, Raisely) being unified into one platform, and that's the honest watch-out: integration between them is newer than the marketing suggests, so check how deeply the pieces actually connect for your workflow before committing. Costs also stack per product and per contact count — a growing donor base raises the CRM bill. For nonprofits though, purpose-built beats adapted business software in fund accounting specifically.

video:video.video:title: VidPal Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Credits don't carry over month to month, and a few users report slow support/account responses — so run the free plan through a full create-and-publish loop before you pay.

video:video.video:title: Vista Social Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It undercuts the big suites convincingly. The honest check is coverage depth: platform APIs change constantly, so verify the specific networks and features YOUR clients need (particularly newer TikTok/threads capabilities and approval workflows) inside the trial rather than trusting the comparison table. Agencies stepping up from Professional hit the Scale tier for white-labeling — price that step into client contracts from day one.

video:video.video:title: Volza Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Three honest catches. The entry plan is narrower than the marketing implies: $1,500 a year covers 182 countries and two users, while the 200-country coverage and ten seats start at $4,500. Downloads run on a credit allowance — 360,000 a year on Startup — and an earlier reading of the catalogue put the cost per record at one credit for US or India shipments and up to ten in thinner markets; that per-country rate is not stated on the current pricing page and we could not re-verify it on 1 September 2026, so treat it as a question for sales rather than a fact. And the update cycle is slow, with some datasets taking up to two months to refresh, which suits structural questions far better than reactive ones. There is a learning curve too; it rewards analysts, not casual users.

video:video.video:title: WP Rocket Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's a subscription, not a lifetime license — you keep your settings if you stop paying but lose updates and support, and a technically-minded user can get most of the way there with a free caching plugin. Two things to check before you buy on price. The Multi licence is capped now: 50, 100 or 500 websites, with a custom licence above that, so there is no unlimited tier to grow into. And the renewal rate is not published — the page confirms the licence auto-renews after a year but never states at what price, which is exactly where the Trustpilot complaints cluster.

video:video.video:title: Warmup Inbox Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing is published and readable — three tiers, per inbox, with both billing toggles printing a rate: $19, $59 and $99 monthly, or $15, $49 and $79 on the yearly plan. The bigger caveat is structural: warmup is priced per inbox, so a team running twenty sending addresses pays twenty times the headline. And warmup is a floor, not a ceiling — it builds sender reputation, but no amount of it rescues a bad list or a bad offer.

video:video.video:title: WebCatalog Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It solves a real annoyance: dozens of web apps and multiple accounts per app as tidy desktop windows. The honest question is whether you need the paid tier at all. The free plan's 2-app limit is tight, but browser profiles and PWAs solve part of the same problem for free. Pro earns its fee when multi-account juggling (several Gmail/Slack/WhatsApp identities) is daily reality.

video:video.video:title: Webflow Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Three separate bills, and the pricing page shows them on separate tabs. A site plan is what puts your site online: $15 a month for a static site, $25 with the CMS. A workspace plan is what lets your team work on it: $19 or $49 a month. And seats are charged on top of the workspace plan at $39 a month each for anyone who can actually design.
