So a two-person team on a CMS site is not $25 a month — it is $25 for the site, $19 for the workspace and $39 for the second seat, which is $83, and that is before add-ons. Two more numbers to find before you commit. The entry ecommerce plan takes a 2% transaction fee on every order, which the $29 headline does not mention and which is the largest single cost for anyone selling real volume; removing it means Plus at $74. And Optimize, the conversion tooling Webflow leads with in its marketing, starts at $299 a month on top of everything else and is priced by page views. Price your team, your site and your add-ons together, because no single tab on that page shows you a total.

video:video.video:title: WebinarGeek Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The friendly €49 headline is the annual rate for just 50 viewers, and the real cost lives in add-ons: localisation, the AI assistant, CRM integrations, RTMP and branding profiles are each €20-59 a month on top, and only a Premium subscription can buy them. A serious webinar stack quickly doubles the base plan.

video:video.video:title: Wegic Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Everything is credits, and generating a site burns them fast — Wegic's own page notes a single generation can cost over $10 in credits, while the free plan gives 100 credits once. The cheaper per-credit rate only kicks in on the higher annual tier, and premium AI media draws down a second 'Cloud' balance on top of your plan.

video:video.video:title: WhatConverts Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The meter is honest and the unit rate is invisible: every phone number, call minute, text, form, chat, appointment, email, event and transaction is charged against a monthly credit, and past that credit WhatConverts publishes no unit price anywhere on its site — the billing FAQ points to a Rates page inside the account. You can still model the bill, just not check the arithmetic: the calculator on the pricing page turns a monthly volume into a usage figure, and on 10 September 2026 it put the $30 Call Tracking plan at no extra usage for 50 calls and 100 forms, $47 at 500 of each and $250 at 2,000 of each. Its genuine strength versus bigger attribution suites is capturing EVERY lead type (not just calls) at a fair price; the flip side is you still need someone to read the reports and reallocate budget, or it's measurement theater.

video:video.video:title: Wing Assistant Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You're renting a person, not automating a task — a good VA is real leverage, but only if you already have documented, delegatable work. Hand over chaos and you'll get chaos back, faster.

video:video.video:title: Wistia Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Bandwidth is the meter that decides your bill, and it is the one number you cannot predict before you publish. A single video that does well can move you from Free to Business in a month, which is arguably the product working — but budget for it rather than being surprised. Their FAQ is precise about which way it cuts: free accounts cannot exceed their bandwidth limit, while paid plans are billed for usage beyond what is included or prepaid. The free tier carries Wistia branding on the player, so it is a trial with no time limit rather than a plan you can ship a brand on. The published prices are the annual ones; the page's toggle sits on Annual with a 20% saving and the month-to-month figures are not in its source, so a monthly subscriber cannot price the plan from the pricing page. The webinar overages are the sharpest edge: $2.00 per extra minute means a session that runs long costs real money, the allowance is per event rather than cumulative, and both facts are in the FAQ rather than on the pricing card.

video:video.video:title: Woodpecker Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $7-per-100-prospects unit reads cheap, but a real outbound motion stacks add-ons fast. Every connected LinkedIn account is $29 a month, managed sending addresses $6 a month apiece and extra warm-ups $5 per account — and contacted prospects are the meter, so scaling outreach scales the bill.

video:video.video:title: Wrike Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's powerful and scales to complex, cross-team portfolios, but that power brings a learning curve and a per-seat cost that climbs — small teams often find it heavier than they need next to a simpler board tool.

video:video.video:title: Xero Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Read the second number, not the first. Every plan on that page is 90% off for six months, and the price that governs the rest of your first year is ten times what the button says: $25, $55 and $90. That is not hidden — it is printed right there — but it is printed smaller, and the plan people pick on the strength of $2.50 a month is the one that becomes $25. Then read the notice further down, because it undercuts even that: Xero says subscription prices are increasing from 1 October 2026, the day after the offer closes, without printing the new rates. So month seven costs $25 or more, and the page will not tell you which. The second thing to check is the entry tier's ceiling: Early is 20 invoices and 5 bills a month, the limit counts approving as well as sending, and connected apps can eat into it on your behalf — which makes Growing at $55 the realistic starting price for anyone billing through other software. And check which country's page you are on, because Xero's tiers and prices differ by market.

video:video.video:title: Zedonk Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The 'starting from' wording is doing real work: £166/mo is the floor of the cheapest module, billed annually, so a working setup for a brand that sells wholesale quickly stacks toward £332/mo and beyond — about £4,000 a year before add-ons. There is no trial and no public total: you find out your actual price in a demo call. Budget for the stack, not the sticker.

video:video.video:title: Zeffy Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The honest scrutiny of 'free': the tip prompt is shown to YOUR donors, with suggested percentages. Most give happily, but some organizations feel it inserts a step between donor and cause — and a donor who tips 10% effectively paid a fee, just voluntarily and not from your share. Compare that trade against the 2-5% the paid platforms take from every donation, and for most small nonprofits the math strongly favors Zeffy.

video:video.video:title: ZenBusiness Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The $0 is real for the filing service and it is also the whole commercial idea: what you sign up for at zero has an annual carry that is not shown next to it. A registered agent is a legal requirement in every state, and theirs is $199/year — so the realistic first-year cost of 'the $0 LLC' is the state fee plus $199, before compliance filing at another $199/year. Price the second year, not the first. The second thing to hold in view is that the state fee is the largest and most variable number in the whole exercise, and ZenBusiness cannot change it. It is set by your state, ranges widely, and their own page sends you to a lookup rather than quoting it. Anyone comparing formation services on the advertised price alone is comparing the small half of the bill.

video:video.video:title: Zendrop Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free plan is a catalogue browser rather than a working tier: it allows no linked products, so nothing can actually be sold through it. Past that you are paying for an allowance, not for capability — Beginner, Pro and Plus carry exactly the same feature list, and the only thing $79 buys over $29 is room for more than a hundred linked products. The subscription is also the smaller half of the bill: product and shipping cost lands per order on top, and Zendrop bills that separately from your Shopify invoice, so the figure you budget is not the figure you pay. Their own pricing page and the App Store listing do not agree: the site sells Free, Pro and Plus with annual rates and no $29 tier, which means the price depends on where you sign up. And the 4.6 average covers a split verdict, with 83% five stars alongside 7% one star across 1,258 reviews — 84 people rating it bottom of the scale.

video:video.video:title: folk Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: One gap has closed and one has narrowed. folk now has a mobile app — the pricing table carries a Mobile app row ticked on all three plans — so the browser-only complaint is out of date. Automation is still uneven, but the picture moved in September: Zapier and Make stay Premium and Enterprise only, and so does the REST API, yet the table now carries an MCP row ticked on all three plans. Standard therefore does have a programmatic route — through an AI client rather than a workflow builder — and no plan shows a native multi-step workflow. Enrichment is capped at 500 a month on Standard and 1,000 on Premium, and email sequences need at least Premium.

video:video.video:title: iContact Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Pricing feels a touch high for what you get, and the Standard plan's hard caps on automations and landing pages push growing teams to upgrade sooner than expected. Set against ActiveCampaign the automation builder is the thinner half of the deal; what iContact sells instead is a product you can hold in your head, deliverability that holds up, and a human on support included rather than sold as a tier.

video:video.video:title: involve.me Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The tier pages sell live funnels, but the meter that empties first is contacts. Start collects 300 contacts a month against 10,000 funnel visits — so a funnel converting at 3% hits the contact ceiling and the visit ceiling in the same week, and the next 200 contacts cost €8.33 on top. Those two meters appear only in the in-app comparison table; the public table publishes the AI-credit allowance but not visits or contacts. The free plan is documented in exactly one place, and not where you would look for it: the pricing FAQ caps it at 50 submissions or 500 visits a month and warns that your funnels lock until the next calendar month if you hit that without upgrading, while the plan cards say nothing at all about what it includes. We measured that part — 2 live funnels, involve.me branding, no team seats — and you only learn it by hitting the wall, because a free account has no usage panel: “Plans & Billing” goes straight to the upgrade page. And the honest fundamental for any interactive-funnel tool: quizzes and calculators convert traffic you already have — they don't create it, so validate on the free plan before the subscription outruns the pipeline.

video:video.video:title: monday.com Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The seat price is not the product price. monday sells four products — Work Management, CRM, Dev and Service — each on its own subscription, and the $9 you see first is the cheapest tier of one of them. A sales team that wants the CRM is buying a second subscription on top of whatever Work Management costs, with a three-seat minimum of its own. The second number to find before you commit is the automation cap. Standard allows 250 automation actions a month across the whole account. If you are buying monday because of the automations you saw demoed, 250 is roughly one workflow running a few times a day — and the next step up is Pro at $19 a seat against Standard's $12. Free is capped at two seats and three boards, which makes it a preview rather than a plan.
